items.stem: A [[who]] has a mass of \([[m]]\,\text{kg}\) and is moving at \([[v]]\,\text{m/s}\). How much energy is in their kinetic energy store?

feedback.no-square: [[wrong]] J multiplies by the speed instead of the speed squared. Square the speed first: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times [[m]] \times [[v]]^{2}\).
feedback.square-mass: [[wrong]] J squares the mass instead of the speed. Only the speed is squared: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times [[m]] \times [[v]]^{2}\).

sample_instances.question_text: A footballer has a mass of \(90\,\text{kg}\) and is moving at \(9\,\text{m/s}\). How much energy is in their kinetic energy store?
A cyclist has a mass of \(70\,\text{kg}\) and is moving at \(8\,\text{m/s}\). How much energy is in their kinetic energy store?

items.question_text: A delivery drone has a mass of 1500 g. It flies horizontally at \(12\,\text{m/s}\). How much energy is in its kinetic energy store?

feedback.a: This multiplies by the speed instead of the speed squared. With the mass in kilograms: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 12^{2} = 108\,\text{J}\).
feedback.b: This squares the mass instead of the speed. Only the speed is squared: \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 12^{2} = 108\,\text{J}\).
feedback.d: This uses the mass in grams. Convert first: 1500 g = 1.5 kg, so \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 12^{2} = 108\,\text{J}\).

items.explanation: Convert the mass to kilograms: 1500 g = 1.5 kg. Then kinetic energy \(= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 12^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1.5 \times 144 = 108\,\text{J}\).

items.question_text: When the speed of a car doubles, the energy in its kinetic energy store undergoes an

options.a: increase by a factor of four

feedback.b: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling the speed multiplies it by 4.
feedback.c: A faster car has more kinetic energy, not less.
feedback.d: A faster car has more kinetic energy, not less.

misconception_map.c: slip: inverted the relationship between speed and energy
misconception_map.d: slip: thinks speeding up reduces kinetic energy

items.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared: doubling the speed multiplies it by 2² = 4.

items.question_text: Car P has twice the mass of car Q. Car Q is moving twice as fast as car P. Which car has more energy in its kinetic energy store?

options.a: Car P, because it has more mass
options.b: Neither: they have the same, because the two effects cancel
options.c: You cannot tell without the actual masses and speeds
options.d: Car Q, because the energy depends on speed squared

feedback.a: Mass matters, but speed matters more: kinetic energy depends on speed squared. Doubling the speed multiplies the energy by 4; doubling the mass only multiplies it by 2. So car Q has twice as much.
feedback.b: The effects would cancel only if kinetic energy depended on speed, not speed squared. Doubling the mass doubles the energy, but doubling the speed multiplies it by 4, so car Q has twice as much.
feedback.c: You can compare without numbers. Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy; doubling the speed multiplies it by 2² = 4. So car Q has twice as much as car P.

misconception_map.a: slip: judged the energy by the mass alone
misconception_map.c: slip: thinks a comparison needs actual values rather than the proportional relationship

items.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass and to speed squared. Car P: 2 × mass, so 2 times the energy. Car Q: 2 × speed, so 2² = 4 times the energy. Car Q has twice as much kinetic energy as car P.

items.question_text: A footballer of mass 80 kg sprints at \(9\,\text{m/s}\). Calculate the energy in her kinetic energy store.

wrong.misconception: Only the speed is squared, not the mass: \(3240\,\text{J}\).
